input: Have you ever wondered how far out a measurement that you read off an instrument might actually be? In this short tutorial, we are going to explore the ideas of absolute error and relative error, and we will do so through a simple flow measurement that makes the distinction nice and concrete. Suppose your flowmeter gives you a reading of 359 units. Every instrument comes with a tolerance, and in this case the tolerance is 0.5% of the reading. What that means in practice is that the absolute error attached to your measurement is 1.79 units: in other words, the true value could sit above or below the figure shown on the display by up to that amount. The relative error, by contrast, expresses the very same tolerance as a fraction of the reading you have taken, which is precisely why it ends up being quoted as a percentage. It is very tempting to use the word uncertainty in exactly the same breath, but it is important to be careful here, because error and uncertainty are not the same thing at all. The error is the difference between the reading and the true value, whereas the uncertainty is the range within which the true value can reasonably be expected to lie, and muddling the two of them up is a surprisingly common source of confusion in practice.
target:
Absolute error and relative error describe the same instrument tolerance in different units, and a flow measurement shows the distinction. A reading of 359 units carries a tolerance of 0.5% of reading. The absolute error is 1.79 units: the difference between the reading and the true value, expressed in the units of the measurement itself. The relative error is that difference divided by the reading, and is dimensionless; stated as a percentage, it is the tolerance in the form in which instrument specifications usually quote it. The two forms convert into each other through the reading, and neither contains information the other lacks.

Error and uncertainty are separate terms and are not interchangeable. Error belongs to a single measurement: it is the difference between the measured value and the true value, and because the true value is not known exactly, the error of a given reading is bounded by the tolerance rather than known outright. Uncertainty belongs to the result as reported: it is the interval, assembled from the tolerance and from every other contribution the measurement carries, within which the true value is asserted to lie. A report that states an error where an uncertainty is meant overstates what the instrument establishes, and a report that merges the two terms leaves the reader unable to tell what has been bounded and what has merely been estimated.
